column4: Those charged to explain the scripture and not conceal it instead cast it وَرَاءَ ظُهُورِهِمْ; this directly joins explanation, concealment, and the section's back-as-forgetting image.
A group given scripture casts God's Book وَرَاءَ ظُهُورِهِمْ as though they did not know, the clearest repeated scene of making revealed remembrance into something left behind.
Shuayb says his people have made God وَرَاءَكُمْ ظِهْرِيًّا; the source section explicitly uses this wording for treating what should remain present as forgotten or neglected.
Receiving one's record وَرَاءَ ظَهْرِهِ turns the discarded-behind-the-back image into a judgment scene: the book once put behind returns behind the person.
God names the revelation ٱلذِّكْرَ and undertakes its preservation, directly realizing the section's linked senses of remembrance, scripture, and guarding.
The promise سَنُقْرِئُكَ فَلَا تَنسَىٰ gives the Prophet recitation without forgetting, matching the section's Quran carried from memory rather than from a written page.
The Reminder is sent to the Prophet لِتُبَيِّنَ لِلنَّاسِ what was revealed, joining zikir-as-book to the section's sense of şerh as public explanation.
God is عَٰلِمُ ٱلْغَيْبِ and does not يُظْهِرُ anyone upon His unseen; the same root that can mean becoming manifest here marks divine control over disclosure.
فَٱذْكُرُونِىٓ أَذْكُرْكُمْ states the reciprocity of remembrance that the section sets against putting someone or something behind one's back.
The person whose breast God has opened to submission is set against hearts hardened مِن ذِكْرِ ٱللَّهِ, bringing شرح الصدر and remembrance into one verse.
God permits houses أَن تُرْفَعَ وَيُذْكَرَ فِيهَا ٱسْمُهُ; raising and a name circulating in speech meet exactly as they do in the section's reading of raised remembrance.
The Prophet is told not to move his tongue hurriedly with the revelation, directly staging the section's image of Quran borne on the tongue.
إِنَّ عَلَيْنَا جَمْعَهُۥ وَقُرْءَانَهُ makes collecting and reciting the revelation God's responsibility, a close parallel to divine preservation and protected memory.
The command to follow the revelation's recitation continues the oral scene and distinguishes faithful reception from casting the Book aside.
ثُمَّ إِنَّ عَلَيْنَا بَيَانَهُ makes its explanation God's undertaking, directly matching the section's dictionary sense of şerh as bayān.
The revelation is ءَايَٰتٌۢ بَيِّنَٰتٌ فِى صُدُورِ those given knowledge: clear signs preserved within breasts are the Quran held without an external book.
People turn revealed scripture into parchments تُبْدُونَهَا وَتُخْفُونَ كَثِيرًا, showing the same book selectively exposed and concealed rather than fully explained.
The Messenger makes clear much that the People of the Book had been hiding, directly moving scripture from concealment to public explanation.
Those who conceal the clear proofs and guidance after God has made them clear in the Book enact the precise failure opposed by the section's opening-and-explaining movement.
After 2:159 condemns concealment, this verse makes reform include وَبَيَّنُوا; its own contribution is the required reversal into active clarification.
The Messenger must convey all that was sent down, while God protects him from people; public delivery and divine guarding meet in one commission.
God tells the Prophet that He narrates earlier reports and has given him مِن لَّدُنَّا ذِكْرًا, identifying the delivered book itself as remembrance.
Whoever turns away from that Reminder will carry وِزْرًا on Resurrection; discarded zikir becoming a carried burden sharply reverses the surah's lifted burden and raised zikir.
The revelation is itself ٱلذِّكْرِ and also كِتَٰبٌ عَزِيزٌ, directly supporting the section's identification of remembrance with the Book.
Continuing 41:41, falsehood cannot reach the Book مِنۢ بَيْنِ يَدَيْهِ وَلَا مِنْ خَلْفِهِۦ; protection from front and behind answers the image of scripture put behind backs.
بَلْ هُوَ قُرْءَانٌ مَّجِيدٌ identifies what is being guarded as the glorious Quran.
فِى لَوْحٍ مَّحْفُوظٍ completes 85:21 with a preserved tablet, giving a concrete scriptural form to the section's guarding sense.
God has made the revelation easy بِلِسَانِكَ so the Prophet may announce and warn; the Book is carried and made public on his tongue.
فَإِنَّمَا يَسَّرْنَٰهُ بِلِسَانِكَ لَعَلَّهُمْ يَتَذَكَّرُونَ explicitly joins revelation made easy on the Prophet's tongue with the hearers' remembering.
God has made the Quran easy لِلذِّكْرِ and asks whether anyone will take reminder, directly linking the Book with retention and recollection.
This repeated declaration again presents the Quran as made easy for remembrance, showing that the invitation to retain it is deliberate and recurrent.
The third repetition renews the same Quran-and-memory relation after another warning narrative.
The fourth repetition closes the sequence by again making remembrance the intended human response to the preserved recitation.
كَلَّآ إِنَّهَا تَذْكِرَةٌ names the revelation a reminder-object, exactly the section's definition of tezkire as that by which something is remembered.
فَمَن شَآءَ ذَكَرَهُۥ states the human act elicited by that reminder: whoever wills keeps it in remembrance.
فِى صُحُفٍ مُّكَرَّمَةٍ locates the reminder of 80:11-12 in honored pages, making the remembered thing explicitly scriptural.
مَّرْفُوعَةٍ مُّطَهَّرَةٍ describes those reminder-pages as raised and purified, an exact meeting of raisedness and scripture-as-zikir.
The revelation is ذِكْرٌ لَّكَ وَلِقَوْمِكَ, meaning reminder and plausibly honor or lasting mention; that semantic overlap directly illuminates the Prophet's raised zikir.
God has sent down كِتَٰبًا فِيهِ ذِكْرُكُمْ; the Book contains the hearers' reminder or mention, joining scripture with the name kept present.
God brought them ذِكْرِهِمْ yet they turn away from their own reminder or honor, a pointed reversal of having one's mention raised and retained.
هَٰذَا ذِكْرُ مَن مَّعِىَ وَذِكْرُ مَن قَبْلِى identifies the present and earlier prophetic scriptures as zikir, matching the source section's dictionary claim about prophets' books.
Abraham asks for لِسَانَ صِدْقٍ فِى ٱلْءَاخِرِينَ, a truthful mention on later tongues; it is a direct nonlexical parallel to an honored name made to endure publicly.
God grants the patriarchs لِسَانَ صِدْقٍ عَلِيًّا, a high truthful mention, bringing tongue, enduring reputation, and elevation into one phrase.
The Messenger complains that his people took this Quran مَهْجُورًا; abandonment is the nonlexical equivalent of putting the Book behind one's back.
Those entrusted with the Torah but failing to bear it are likened to a donkey carrying books, a sharp counterimage to scripture truly carried in memory and speech.
People recite the Book yet تَنسَوْنَ أَنفُسَكُمْ; recitation without retained self-application exposes the gap between a book on the tongue and remembrance in the person.
وَٱذْكُر رَّبَّكَ إِذَا نَسِيتَ places remembering directly after forgetting, stating the lexical opposition developed in the section.
Joseph asks a companion ٱذْكُرْنِى عِندَ رَبِّكَ, but Satan makes him forget that mention; a name meant to travel on a tongue is instead withheld by forgetting.
One reminded of God's signs turns away and وَنَسِىَ مَا قَدَّمَتْ يَدَاهُ, joining offered reminder, physical aversion, and forgetting.
The reply says God's signs came but the person forgot them, so today he is forgotten; remembrance rejected becomes reciprocal forgetting.
Satan makes a people forget ذِكْرَ ٱللَّهِ, explicitly placing induced forgetting against remembrance.
Those who forgot God were made to forget themselves, a reciprocal reversal that darkens the promise أَذْكُرْكُمْ in 2:152.
نَسُوا۟ ٱللَّهَ فَنَسِيَهُمْ gives another reciprocal forgetting scene, the negative counterpart to mutual remembrance.
Covenant-breakers distort words and نَسُوا۟ حَظًّا مِّمَّا ذُكِّرُوا۟ بِهِۦ, forgetting a portion of what they were reminded, as though setting revelation behind them.
A second covenant community likewise forgets part of what it was reminded, showing the same movement from entrusted word to neglected memory.
فَلَمَّا نَسُوا۟ مَا ذُكِّرُوا۟ بِهِۦ directly joins forgetting with the reminder previously given; the ensuing opening of worldly gates makes the neglect temporarily look like ease.
When the transgressors forget what they had been reminded of, God rescues those who forbade evil; retained reminder here becomes a dividing line.
يَشْرَحْ صَدْرَهُۥ لِلْإِسْلَٰمِ repeats the opening of a breast as the act by which God makes a person fit for guidance.
Moses prays رَبِّ ٱشْرَحْ لِى صَدْرِى, the exact breast-opening image voiced by another messenger before his public task.
The qualification after 87:6 says God knows ٱلْجَهْرَ وَمَا يَخْفَىٰ, joining protected recitation with His knowledge of what is spoken openly and what remains hidden.
The exception to 72:26 allows disclosure of the unseen to a chosen messenger and stations guards around him; hidden knowledge becomes guarded revelation.
The guarded disclosure serves that messengers have delivered their Lord's messages, completing the sequence from hidden knowledge to protected public communication.
Gabriel brought the revelation عَلَىٰ قَلْبِكَ by God's permission, a direct Quranic counterpart to carrying the Quran inwardly in the heart.
The trustworthy Spirit brings the revelation عَلَىٰ قَلْبِكَ so the Prophet may warn, linking inward reception to outward speech.
بِلِسَانٍ عَرَبِىٍّ مُّبِينٍ completes the heart-reception scene with a clear Arabic tongue, moving the revelation from inwardly held to manifest speech.
Every person's record is fastened to the neck and brought out on Resurrection as an open book, making what was carried and hidden into a visible record.
ٱقْرَأْ كِتَٰبَكَ commands the person to read that opened record, so the book itself makes forgotten deeds present to consciousness.
فَمَا لَهُمْ عَنِ ٱلتَّذْكِرَةِ مُعْرِضِينَ asks why they turn bodily and mentally away from the reminder, closely matching scripture put behind the back.
كَأَنَّهُمْ حُمُرٌ مُّسْتَنفِرَةٌ gives the turners-away a visible herd image; its contribution is the panic embodied in their rejection of reminder.
فَرَّتْ مِن قَسْوَرَةٍ completes the fleeing-herd comparison, showing how emphatically the reminder has been put behind them.
كَلَّآ إِنَّهُۥ تَذْكِرَةٌ reasserts that the very revelation from which they flee is a reminder-object.
فَمَن شَآءَ ذَكَرَهُۥ answers flight with the possibility of retaining the reminder in mind.
The Prophet was not taught poetry; the revelation is إِلَّا ذِكْرٌ وَقُرْءَانٌ مُّبِينٌ, explicitly joining Reminder, Quran, and manifest clarity.
The question whether every covenant is made only for a party to cast it away begins the discard scene that 2:101 specifies as putting the Book behind their backs.
Those who conceal what God sent down of the Book turn revealed guidance back into hidden material for a petty price.
The People of the Book are asked why they conceal truth knowingly, a direct failure to make entrusted revelation manifest.
A group twists its tongues with scripture so listeners think their speech belongs to the Book; the tongue carries revelation falsely rather than preserving and explaining it.
Some distort words and twist their tongues in religion, another corrupted form of carrying the sacred word orally.
Every messenger is sent in his people's language لِيُبَيِّنَ لَهُمْ, making clear speech the public function of revelation.
The Book is sent to the Prophet only لِتُبَيِّنَ لَهُمُ what they dispute, repeating the explanatory commission of 16:44.
The Prophet is commanded فَحَدِّثْ of his Lord's favor, another movement from a received gift into openly circulating speech.
The revelation is a Book whose verses have been fully set out as an Arabic Quran for people who know, embodying scripture made clear.
Although 41:3 presents an explained Book, most people turn away and do not listen; their refusal reverses the intended movement from revelation to hearing.
مَن شَرَحَ بِٱلْكُفْرِ صَدْرًا uses the same breast-opening form for willing unbelief, a precise moral reversal of the opened breast in 94:1 and 6:125.
The lost carry their burdens عَلَىٰ ظُهُورِهِمْ; a back crushed by burdens is the concrete opposite of the surah's back relieved so remembrance can be raised.
Receiving the record in the right hand provides the explicit favorable counterpart to 84:10's record handed from behind the back.
God could remove the revelation from the Prophet and leave no guardian for it; this stated possibility marks the boundary around the preservation promised in 15:9.
Israel is commanded to hold the revealed gift firmly and remember what is in it, the exact positive reversal of throwing scripture behind the back.
Under the raised mountain, the community is told to hold the Book firmly and remember its contents, setting retention against later scriptural forgetting.
The command to hold the covenant firmly and listen is answered with “we hear and disobey,” exposing the refusal that precedes casting the Book away.
Those who recite the Book with its true recitation embody the opposite of treating it as a load carried without faithful retention.
The person given the record in the left hand wishes it had never been received, another judgment reversal of scripture as honored reminder.
The wall's بَاطِنُهُ contains mercy while its ظَاهِرُهُ faces punishment, giving the hidden/manifest pair sharply opposite contents.
Those who forgot the meeting of their day are “forgotten” that day, a judgment reversal of reciprocal remembrance.
“Today We forget you as you forgot the meeting of this day” turns chosen forgetfulness into experienced abandonment.
The same reciprocal verdict is stated again: rejection and forgetting of the meeting result in being left forgotten.
The recipient of the book from behind the back calls for destruction; this verse supplies the immediate human consequence of the posture in 84:10.
Entering the Blaze completes the adverse book-behind-back scene begun in 84:10.
The person handed the record in the right hand publicly invites others to read it, turning a private record into glad, open proclamation.
The Prophet is told to recite the revealed Book, whose words no one can change; oral delivery and textual preservation meet here.
إِنَّهُۥ لَقُرْءَانٌ كَرِيمٌ identifies the noble recitation before the next verse locates it within a concealed book.
فِى كِتَٰبٍ مَّكْنُونٍ places the recited Quran in a hidden or protected Book, a boundary between concealed source and voiced revelation.
The Quran is delivered gradually لِنُثَبِّتَ بِهِۦ فُؤَادَكَ and recited distinctly, linking ordered recitation with the Prophet's inward firmness.
Each challenge is answered with truth and أَحْسَنَ تَفْسِيرًا; the verse contributes the revelation's explanatory response to what is brought forward.
The Quran is divided so the Prophet may recite it to people over time, showing a stored revelation made public through repeated speech.
After 39:22 joins opened breast and remembrance, this verse calls revelation the best discourse, a consistent Book, and describes hearts softening to God's remembrance.
Abraham makes the declaration a word lasting among his descendants so they may return, a concrete model of speech preserved across generations.
God leaves Noah's truthful mention among later generations, a direct example of a prophet's name being preserved after him.
The same formula leaves Abraham's mention among later peoples, realizing the enduring tongue-of-truth he requested in 26:84.
Moses and Aaron likewise receive a mention left among later generations, extending the pattern of divinely sustained prophetic memory.
Elijah's mention is also left among later generations, another instance of a prophetic name made to remain in communal speech.
God and the angels bless the Prophet and believers are commanded to bless and greet him, a concrete practice by which his mention continually circulates.
The Prophet's household is told to remember what is recited in their homes of God's signs and wisdom, joining oral recitation with deliberate retention.
In the witnessing rule, if one woman errs the other تُذَكِّرَ her, using remembrance as the act that restores something liable to be lost.
God has enumerated the deeds that people forgot, showing divine preservation bringing forgotten acts back into view on the Day of Resurrection.
The record is set down and omits nothing small or great; what people may have forgotten remains preserved and visibly present.
وَإِذَا ٱلصُّحُفُ نُشِرَتْ pictures records spread open, a material version of what was hidden becoming public and readable.
The oath by a written Book makes the remembered word a fixed inscription.
فِى رَقٍّ مَّنشُورٍ adds an unrolled, spread-open parchment, bringing written preservation into manifest view.
God is ٱلظَّٰهِرُ وَٱلْبَاطِنُ, the Quran's most compressed pairing of the manifest and the hidden.
The command to leave both ظَٰهِرَ ٱلْإِثْمِ وَبَاطِنَهُ applies the manifest/hidden distinction to sin.
The forbidden indecencies include مَا ظَهَرَ مِنْهَا وَمَا بَطَنَ, again marking the boundary between what appears and what remains concealed.
God's favors are bestowed ظَٰهِرَةً وَبَاطِنَةً, using the same outer/hidden polarity for gifts rather than for words.
Whether people hide or disclose what is in their breasts, God knows it; inward content and outward manifestation meet at the chest.
God knows what people conceal and declare and knows what breasts contain, another direct passage from inward storage to outward speech.
Whether speech is kept secret or voiced openly, God knows what is within breasts; tongue, hiddenness, and inward keeping are held together.
يَوْمَ تُبْلَى ٱلسَّرَآئِرُ names the day when inner secrets are exposed or tested, a broad eschatological realization of hidden becoming manifest.
وَحُصِّلَ مَا فِى ٱلصُّدُورِ brings out what is inside breasts, reversing inward concealment into disclosure.
ظَهَرَ ٱلْفَسَادُ describes corruption becoming manifest on land and sea; it uses the section's emergence sense of ظهر for an adverse thing made visible.
The Messenger's duty is delivery while God knows what people disclose and conceal, placing public proclamation beside divine knowledge of both directions.
God hears secret speech and private counsel while His messengers write it down, turning hidden words into a preserved record.
God knows speech spoken aloud and what people conceal, applying the open/hidden distinction specifically to utterance.
God knows both what hostile speakers conceal and what they declare, so unvoiced and voiced words are equally present to Him.
The scripture given to Moses and Aaron is called criterion, illumination, and ذِكْرًا, supporting the section's claim that earlier prophetic books are remembrances.
God says He wrote in the Psalms after ٱلذِّكْرِ, where zikir denotes an antecedent divine record or scripture rather than merely an act of remembering.
Those who do not know are directed to أَهْلَ ٱلذِّكْرِ, the people who possess earlier revealed knowledge.
The repeated instruction to ask أَهْلَ ٱلذِّكْرِ again uses zikir for the body of remembered scriptural knowledge held by a community.
وَهَٰذَا ذِكْرٌ مُّبَارَكٌ أَنزَلْنَٰهُ calls the present revelation a blessed Reminder that has been sent down.
The ark-event is made تَذْكِرَةً and retained by أُذُنٌ وَٰعِيَةٌ; a reminder-object and the organ that preserves it are explicitly paired.
The Quran is called تَذْكِرَةٌ لِّلْمُتَّقِينَ, directly exemplifying a reminder as the thing by which truth is recalled.
إِنَّ هَٰذِهِۦ تَذْكِرَةٌ presents the recited warning itself as a reminder that can guide a chosen path.
The discourse is again called تَذْكِرَةٌ, with remembering meant to lead the hearer toward the Lord.
فَذَكِّرْ إِنَّمَآ أَنتَ مُذَكِّرٌ gives the Prophet the role of actively bringing the reminder to mind through speech.
The Prophet is told to remind because remembrance benefits believers, emphasizing zikir as an outward act that preserves an inward truth.
Whenever a renewed reminder comes from their Lord, people listen while playing, so delivered revelation reaches the ear without being kept.
No renewed reminder comes from the Merciful without their turning away, a recurring scripture-behind-the-back movement.
The question whether God should turn ٱلذِّكْرَ away from a transgressing people reverses the usual scene: here withholding revelation is posed as a divine response.
When the Prophet mentions his Lord alone in the Quran, opponents turn عَلَىٰٓ أَدْبَٰرِهِمْ in aversion, bodily putting the spoken reminder behind them.
The person reminded of the Lord's signs then turns away enacts the same sequence as receiving and discarding scripture.
The Quran is repeatedly varied لِيَذَّكَّرُوا۟, yet the hearers increase in aversion; abundant reminder does not guarantee retained remembrance.
The warning has been distributed among people لِيَذَّكَّرُوا۟, but most refuse except in ingratitude, contrasting dissemination with reception.

Entering houses مِن ظُهُورِهَا is rejected in favor of entering through their doors, a concrete back-to-proper-entrance movement that echoes the section's passage from behind to what is brought forward.
The command not to conceal truth knowingly names concealment as an active covering of what should be made clear.
Moses says the knowledge is in a Book with his Lord and that his Lord neither errs nor forgets, uniting written record with unfailing divine memory.
وَمَا كَانَ رَبُّكَ نَسِيًّا assures the Prophet that his Lord is never forgetful, a boundary around the fear of neglected need or delayed revelation.
Joseph's former companion remembers him after a long interval, completing the delayed name-on-the-tongue scene begun in 12:42.
The servant reports forgetting the fish and being made to forget أَنْ أَذْكُرَهُ, again putting mention and forgetting in the same small scene.
مَا وَدَّعَكَ رَبُّكَ وَمَا قَلَىٰ assures the same Prophet that his Lord has not abandoned him, the personal counterpart to a need not put behind the back.
God raises Idris مَكَانًا عَلِيًّا; this is a different, personal use of elevation that helps distinguish raised station from raised public mention.
God raises believers and those given knowledge in degrees, another honor-bestowing sense of رفع alongside the section's sense of making mention public.
God sends the Messenger with guidance and truth لِيُظْهِرَهُۥ عَلَى ٱلدِّينِ كُلِّهِۦ; the causative of ظهر moves the message into public prevalence, beyond mere visibility.
The same promise that the true religion will be made manifest or prevailing repeats the public expansion side of the ظهر root.
A third occurrence again links the Messenger's mission with making the true religion manifest over all religion.
The opponents allege a human teacher, but the revelation is identified as a clear Arabic tongue, stressing the public linguistic vehicle by which it is borne.
